claim: Individual neurons can undergo drastic structural changes, known as neuronal remodeling or structural plasticity.
source: Individual neurons can undergo drastic structural changes, known as neuronal remodeling or structural plasticity.
evidence: This is a general statement about neuronal biology presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Neuronal remodeling occurs in response to hormones, such as during puberty in mammals or metamorphosis in insects.
source: One example of this is in response to hormones, such as during puberty in mammals or metamorphosis in insects.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific knowledge about hormone-induced neuronal changes.

claim: It remains unclear whether remodeled neurons resume prior patterns of connectivity.
source: However, in each of these examples, it remains unclear whether the remodeled neuron resumes prior patterns of connectivity, and if so, whether the persistent circuits drive similar behaviors.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, identifying a gap.

claim: Larval MDN induces backward crawling.
source: We previously showed that larval MDN induces backward crawling, and synapses onto the Pair1 interneuron to inhibit forward crawling (Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Larval MDN synapses onto the Pair1 interneuron to inhibit forward crawling.
source: We previously showed that larval MDN induces backward crawling, and synapses onto the Pair1 interneuron to inhibit forward crawling (Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: MDN is remodeled during metamorphosis.
source: MDN is remodeled during metamorphosis and regulates backward walking in the adult fly.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact from prior work.

claim: MDN regulates backward walking in the adult fly.
source: MDN is remodeled during metamorphosis and regulates backward walking in the adult fly.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact from prior work.

claim: Pair1 is remodeled during metamorphosis and persists in the adult fly.
source: We assayed morphology and molecular markers to demonstrate that Pair1 is remodeled during metamorphosis and persists in the adult fly.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological and molecular marker data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MDN-Pair1 connectivity is lost during early pupal stages when both neurons are severely pruned back.
source: MDN-Pair1 connectivity is lost during early pupal stages, when both neurons are severely pruned back, but connectivity is re-established at mid-pupal stages and persist into the adult.
evidence: This claim is supported by t-GRASP data showing absence of connectivity at 24 hr APF.

claim: MDN-Pair1 connectivity is re-established at mid-pupal stages and persists into the adult.
source: MDN-Pair1 connectivity is lost during early pupal stages, when both neurons are severely pruned back, but connectivity is re-established at mid-pupal stages and persist into the adult.
evidence: This claim is supported by t-GRASP data showing connectivity at 48 hr APF and in adults.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Pair1 in the adult results in arrest of forward locomotion.
source: In the adult, optogenetic activation of Pair1 resulted in arrest of forward locomotion, similar to what is observed in larvae.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Adult Pair1 activation produces similar locomotor effects as larval Pair1 activation.
source: In the adult, optogenetic activation of Pair1 resulted in arrest of forward locomotion, similar to what is observed in larvae.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of adult behavioral data with previously published larval data.

claim: The MDN-Pair1 neurons are an interneuronal circuit that is re-established during metamorphosis yet generates similar locomotor behavior at both larval and adult stages.
source: Thus, the MDN-Pair1 neurons are an interneuronal circuit – a pair of synaptically connected interneurons – that is re-established during metamorphosis, yet generates similar locomotor behavior at both larval and adult stages.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the combined morphological, connectivity, and behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Large-scale changes in neuronal morphology and function occur during mammalian puberty.
source: Large-scale changes in neuronal morphology and function occur during mammalian puberty (Barendse et al., 2018; Mills et al., 2016; Sisk and Zehr, 2005), as well as several neurobiological disorders including depression (Patel et al., 2019), or chronic pain (Kuner and Flor, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Large-scale changes in neuronal morphology and function occur in neurobiological disorders including depression.
source: Large-scale changes in neuronal morphology and function occur during mammalian puberty (Barendse et al., 2018; Mills et al., 2016; Sisk and Zehr, 2005), as well as several neurobiological disorders including depression (Patel et al., 2019), or chronic pain (Kuner and Flor, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Large-scale changes in neuronal morphology and function occur in chronic pain.
source: Large-scale changes in neuronal morphology and function occur during mammalian puberty (Barendse et al., 2018; Mills et al., 2016; Sisk and Zehr, 2005), as well as several neurobiological disorders including depression (Patel et al., 2019), or chronic pain (Kuner and Flor, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Major changes in neuronal numbers and type occur as a result of insect metamorphosis.
source: Similarly, major changes in neuronal numbers and type occur as a result of insect metamorphosis (Kanamori et al., 2015; Truman and Reiss, 1976; Yaniv and Schuldiner, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Individual insect neurons can persist from larval to adult stages.
source: Despite these changes, there are documented cases of individual insect neurons persisting from larval to adult stages.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: In Drosophila, individual motor and sensory neurons persist throughout metamorphosis and undergo dramatic remodeling.
source: In Drosophila, individual motor and sensory neurons have been shown to persist throughout metamorphosis and undergo dramatic remodeling (Consoulas et al., 2002; Consoulas et al., 2000; Yaniv and Schuldiner, 2016; Yu and Schuldiner, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Kenyon cell partners (projection neurons, DANs) exist at both larval and adult stages in the insect mushroom body.
source: Similar findings have been reported for the insect mushroom body, where Kenyon cells partners (projection neurons, DANs) exist at both larval and adult stages (Li et al., 2020; Marin et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: It remains unclear whether remodeled neurons re-establish connectivity with the identical neurons in the larva and adult.
source: Yet, it remains unclear whether the remodeled neurons re-establish connectivity with the identical neurons in the larva and adult.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, identifying a gap.

claim: During Drosophila metamorphosis, the animal changes from a crawling limbless larva to a walking six-legged adult.
source: During Drosophila metamorphosis, the animal changes from a crawling limbless larva to a walking six-legged adult (Riddiford, 1980; Riddiford et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about Drosophila development, supported by citations.

claim: Both larvae and adults undergo forward locomotion in search of food.
source: Despite the obvious differences, some behaviors are similar: both larvae and adults undergo forward locomotion in search of food, backward locomotion in response to noxious stimuli, and pausing in between antagonistic behaviors (Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Both larvae and adults undergo backward locomotion in response to noxious stimuli.
source: Despite the obvious differences, some behaviors are similar: both larvae and adults undergo forward locomotion in search of food, backward locomotion in response to noxious stimuli, and pausing in between antagonistic behaviors (Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Both larvae and adults pause in between antagonistic behaviors.
source: Despite the obvious differences, some behaviors are similar: both larvae and adults undergo forward locomotion in search of food, backward locomotion in response to noxious stimuli, and pausing in between antagonistic behaviors (Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A neuron named moonwalker descending neuron (MDN) can trigger backward locomotion in both larvae and adults when activated.
source: We and others identified a neuron that, when activated, can trigger backward locomotion in both larvae and adults (Bidaye et al., 2014; Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018; Sen et al., 2017), despite the obvious differences in limbless and six-legged locomotion.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: MDN is present as a bilateral neuronal pair in each brain lobe.
source: This neuron, named mooncrawler/moonwalker descending neuron (MDN), is present as a bilateral neuronal pair in each brain lobe, with all four MDNs having similar synaptic partners, and all four MDNs capable of eliciting backward larval locomotion in larvae (Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: All four MDNs have similar synaptic partners.
source: This neuron, named mooncrawler/moonwalker descending neuron (MDN), is present as a bilateral neuronal pair in each brain lobe, with all four MDNs having similar synaptic partners, and all four MDNs capable of eliciting backward larval locomotion in larvae (Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: All four MDNs are capable of eliciting backward larval locomotion in larvae.
source: This neuron, named mooncrawler/moonwalker descending neuron (MDN), is present as a bilateral neuronal pair in each brain lobe, with all four MDNs having similar synaptic partners, and all four MDNs capable of eliciting backward larval locomotion in larvae (Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Larval MDNs function within a neural circuit that induces backward locomotion and coordinately arrests forward locomotion.
source: Larval MDNs function within a neural circuit that induces backward locomotion and coordinately arrests forward locomotion.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact from prior work.

claim: Halting forward locomotion is achieved via activation of the Pair1 descending interneuron, which inhibits the A27h premotor neuron.
source: Halting forward locomotion is achieved via activation of the Pair1 descending interneuron, which inhibits the A27h premotor neuron.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The A27h interneuron is required for forward locomotion.
source: Given that the A27h interneuron is required for forward locomotion, its inhibition via MDN-induced Pair1 activation prevents forward locomotion (Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Inhibition of A27h via MDN-induced Pair1 activation prevents forward locomotion.
source: Given that the A27h interneuron is required for forward locomotion, its inhibition via MDN-induced Pair1 activation prevents forward locomotion (Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Activating backward locomotion is likely due, in part, to MDN activation of the A18b premotor neuron.
source: Activating backward locomotion is likely to be due, in part, to MDN activation of the A18b premotor neuron, which is specifically active during backward locomotion (Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim involves speculation ('likely') but is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A18b premotor neuron is specifically active during backward locomotion.
source: Activating backward locomotion is likely to be due, in part, to MDN activation of the A18b premotor neuron, which is specifically active during backward locomotion (Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: MDN-Pair1 are synaptically coupled members of a locomotor circuit in the Drosophila larva.
source: Thus, MDN-Pair1 are synaptically coupled members of a locomotor circuit in the Drosophila larva.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Larval Pair1 neurons have characteristic cell body position in the medial subesophageal zone (SEZ).
source: We identified the larval Pair1 neurons based on their characteristic cell body position in the medial subesophageal zone (SEZ), dense local ipsilateral dendritic arborizations (defined as dendritic based on enrichment for post-synapses in the TEM reconstruction of the larval Pair1 neuron; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and contralateral axons descending into the ventral nerve cord (VNC) in an extremely lateral axon tract (Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological observations and TEM data.

claim: Larval Pair1 neurons have dense local ipsilateral dendritic arborizations.
source: We identified the larval Pair1 neurons based on their characteristic cell body position in the medial subesophageal zone (SEZ), dense local ipsilateral dendritic arborizations (defined as dendritic based on enrichment for post-synapses in the TEM reconstruction of the larval Pair1 neuron; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and contralateral axons descending into the ventral nerve cord (VNC) in an extremely lateral axon tract (Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological observations and TEM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Larval Pair1 dendritic domains are defined as dendritic based on enrichment for post-synapses in the TEM reconstruction.
source: We identified the larval Pair1 neurons based on their characteristic cell body position in the medial subesophageal zone (SEZ), dense local ipsilateral dendritic arborizations (defined as dendritic based on enrichment for post-synapses in the TEM reconstruction of the larval Pair1 neuron; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and contralateral axons descending into the ventral nerve cord (VNC) in an extremely lateral axon tract (Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Larval Pair1 neurons have contralateral axons descending into the ventral nerve cord (VNC) in an extremely lateral axon tract.
source: We identified the larval Pair1 neurons based on their characteristic cell body position in the medial subesophageal zone (SEZ), dense local ipsilateral dendritic arborizations (defined as dendritic based on enrichment for post-synapses in the TEM reconstruction of the larval Pair1 neuron; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and contralateral axons descending into the ventral nerve cord (VNC) in an extremely lateral axon tract (Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological observations and citation to prior work.

claim: Pair1 neurons with characteristic morphology can be identified at 28 and 96 hr after larval hatching (ALH).
source: Using the Pair1-Gal4 line, we could identify Pair1 neurons with this morphology at 28 and 96 hr after larval hatching (ALH; Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: At 24 hr after pupal formation (APF), Pair1 neuron cell bodies and proximal neurites can still be observed, but virtually all of the dendritic processes and descending axonal process are pruned.
source: The Pair1 neuron cell bodies and proximal neurites could still be observed at 24 hr after pupal formation (APF), but virtually all of the dendridic processes and descending axonal process are pruned (Figure 1C, only one neuron labeled).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Many or all neurons undergo axon/dendrite remodeling during metamorphosis.
source: This is expected, given that many or all neurons undergo axon/dendrite remodeling during metamorphosis (Kanamori et al., 2015; Truman and Reiss, 1976; Yaniv and Schuldiner, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: At 48 hr APF, Pair1 neurons exhibit dendritic branching in the SEZ and a descending axon into the VNC, regaining morphological features similar to that of larval Pair1 neurons.
source: At 48 hr APF, Pair1 neurons exhibited dendritic branching in the SEZ and a descending axon into the VNC, regaining morphological features similar to that of larval Pair1 neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At 48 hr APF, the Pair1 axon innervates the T1 (prothoracic) neuropil and descends further down the VNC.
source: The axon innervated the T1 (prothoracic) neuropil and descended further down the VNC.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological observations from confocal imaging.

claim: Pair1 morphological features are maintained into the adult fly.
source: These morphological features were maintained into the adult fly, where we could trace the Pair1 axon to primarily innervate the T1 neuropil (Figure 1E), with less extensive innervation of the mesothoracic (T2) and metathoracic (T3) neuropils.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In the adult, the Pair1 axon primarily innervates the T1 neuropil, with less extensive innervation of the T2 and T3 neuropils.
source: These morphological features were maintained into the adult fly, where we could trace the Pair1 axon to primarily innervate the T1 neuropil (Figure 1E), with less extensive innervation of the mesothoracic (T2) and metathoracic (T3) neuropils.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Larval Pair1 neurons permanently labeled at 96 hr ALH are present in the 4-day old adult.
source: We immortalized Pair1 neurons in the larva, and assayed expression in the adult, and observed the two bilateral Pair1 neurons, based on characteristic medial SEZ cell body position, local ipsilateral arbors, and contralateral descending axons that preferentially innervate the prothoracic neuropil (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immortalization experiments and confocal imaging shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Immortalization of Pair1 during larval stages reduces off-target neuron expression in the adult VNC and reveals greatly enriched innervation in the T1 neuropil.
source: Pair1 innervation is clearer in neurons immortalized during larval stages, which reduces the off-target neuron expression in the adult VNC, and reveals an greatly enriched level of innervation in the T1 neuropil (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of immortalization data with standard Gal4 expression patterns.

claim: Larval and adult Pair1 neurons express Hunchback (Hb).
source: Larval and adult Pair1 neurons expressed Hunchback (Hb), Sex combs reduced (Scr), and Bicoid (Bcd); but did not express Visual system homeobox (Vsx1) or Nab (Figure 2A–N).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Larval and adult Pair1 neurons express Sex combs reduced (Scr).
source: Larval and adult Pair1 neurons expressed Hunchback (Hb), Sex combs reduced (Scr), and Bicoid (Bcd); but did not express Visual system homeobox (Vsx1) or Nab (Figure 2A–N).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Larval and adult Pair1 neurons express Bicoid (Bcd).
source: Larval and adult Pair1 neurons expressed Hunchback (Hb), Sex combs reduced (Scr), and Bicoid (Bcd); but did not express Visual system homeobox (Vsx1) or Nab (Figure 2A–N).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Larval and adult Pair1 neurons do not express Visual system homeobox (Vsx1).
source: Larval and adult Pair1 neurons expressed Hunchback (Hb), Sex combs reduced (Scr), and Bicoid (Bcd); but did not express Visual system homeobox (Vsx1) or Nab (Figure 2A–N).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Larval and adult Pair1 neurons do not express Nab.
source: Larval and adult Pair1 neurons expressed Hunchback (Hb), Sex combs reduced (Scr), and Bicoid (Bcd); but did not express Visual system homeobox (Vsx1) or Nab (Figure 2A–N).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: There are many other Scr/Bcd/Hb triple-positive neurons in the SEZ.
source: However, there were many other Scr/Bcd/Hb triple-positive neurons in the SEZ (Figure 2O,P), showing that additional factors would be necessary to uniquely specify Pair1 identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 2O,P.

claim: Additional factors beyond Hb, Bcd, and Scr would be necessary to uniquely specify Pair1 identity.
source: However, there were many other Scr/Bcd/Hb triple-positive neurons in the SEZ (Figure 2O,P), showing that additional factors would be necessary to uniquely specify Pair1 identity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that many neurons share the same three transcription factors.

claim: The three transcription factors (Hb, Bcd, Scr) may be part of a molecular code that directs both larval and adult Pair1 morphology and/or connectivity.
source: These results support the conclusion that Pair1 persists from larva to adult, maintaining both molecular and morphological features, and raises the interesting possibility that the three TFs (Hb, Bcd, Scr) may be part of a molecular code that directs both larval and adult Pair1 morphology and/or connectivity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential function of the transcription factors.

claim: Control flies exposed to red light did not pause or arrest forward locomotion.
source: Control flies exposed to red light did not pause or arrest forward locomotion, did not show an increased probability of pausing, and did not have a decrease in distance traveled during the stimulus interval.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from control experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Control flies exposed to red light did not show an increased probability of pausing.
source: Control flies exposed to red light did not pause or arrest forward locomotion, did not show an increased probability of pausing, and did not have a decrease in distance traveled during the stimulus interval.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from control experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Control flies exposed to red light did not have a decrease in distance traveled during the stimulus interval.
source: Control flies exposed to red light did not pause or arrest forward locomotion, did not show an increased probability of pausing, and did not have a decrease in distance traveled during the stimulus interval.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from control experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Experimental flies expressing Chrimson in Pair1 neurons showed a near-complete arrest of forward locomotion.
source: In contrast, experimental flies expressing Chrimson in Pair1 neurons showed a near-complete arrest of forward locomotion, an increased probability of pausing, and a reduced distance traveled during the stimulus interval (Figure 3A–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Experimental flies expressing Chrimson in Pair1 neurons showed an increased probability of pausing.
source: In contrast, experimental flies expressing Chrimson in Pair1 neurons showed a near-complete arrest of forward locomotion, an increased probability of pausing, and a reduced distance traveled during the stimulus interval (Figure 3A–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Experimental flies expressing Chrimson in Pair1 neurons showed a reduced distance traveled during the stimulus interval.
source: In contrast, experimental flies expressing Chrimson in Pair1 neurons showed a near-complete arrest of forward locomotion, an increased probability of pausing, and a reduced distance traveled during the stimulus interval (Figure 3A–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effects of Pair1 activation were reversed after turning off the red light, with the exception of a slightly reduced distance traveled.
source: These effects were reversed after turning off the red light, with the exception of a slightly reduced distance traveled, likely due to a lingering physiological effect of the 30 s Pair1 activation (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: The slightly reduced distance traveled after light offset is likely due to a lingering physiological effect of the 30 s Pair1 activation.
source: These effects were reversed after turning off the red light, with the exception of a slightly reduced distance traveled, likely due to a lingering physiological effect of the 30 s Pair1 activation (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: Pair1 activation resulted in an increase in immobile flies.
source: Pair1 activation resulted in an increase in immobile flies (Figure 3E) and a corresponding decrease in whole body translocation (Figure 3F, defined as 'large movements').
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Pair1 activation resulted in a decrease in whole body translocation (defined as 'large movements').
source: Pair1 activation resulted in an increase in immobile flies (Figure 3E) and a corresponding decrease in whole body translocation (Figure 3F, defined as 'large movements').
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Pair1 activation did not prevent small body part movements such as those involved in grooming.
source: Importantly, Pair1 activation did not prevent small body part movements such as those involved in grooming (Figure 3G, defined as 'small movements').
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The arrest in forward locomotion is due to Chrimson activation of the Pair1 neurons.
source: Note that Pair1-Gal4 off-target expression is common but variable from fly to fly, whereas its expression in Pair1 neurons is fully penetrant; because the Chrimson-induced behavior is also fully penetrant, we conclude that the arrest in forward locomotion is due to Chrimson activation of the Pair1 neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the penetrance of Pair1 expression and the behavioral phenotype.

claim: Pair1 activation prevents a single behavior – forward locomotion – but does not produce general paralysis or interfere with non-translocating limb movements.
source: We conclude that Pair1 activation prevents a single behavior – forward locomotion – but does not produce general paralysis or interfere with non-translocating limb movements.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the behavioral data presented.

claim: MDN and Pair1 neurites are in close proximity to each other in the adult.
source: We observed MDN and Pair1 neurites in close proximity to each other (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: MDN-Pair1 connectivity was absent at 24 hr APF when neurite pruning was maximal.
source: MDN-Pair1 connectivity was absent at 24 hr APF (Figure 4F,G) when neurite pruning was maximal (Figure 1C), but was re-established at 48 hr APF (Figure 4H,I) when neurite regrowth was occurring (Figure 1D) and maintained into the adult (Figure 4J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by t-GRASP data shown in Figure 4F,G.

claim: MDN-Pair1 connectivity was re-established at 48 hr APF when neurite regrowth was occurring.
source: MDN-Pair1 connectivity was absent at 24 hr APF (Figure 4F,G) when neurite pruning was maximal (Figure 1C), but was re-established at 48 hr APF (Figure 4H,I) when neurite regrowth was occurring (Figure 1D) and maintained into the adult (Figure 4J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by t-GRASP data shown in Figure 4H,I.

claim: MDN-Pair1 connectivity is maintained into the adult.
source: MDN-Pair1 connectivity was absent at 24 hr APF (Figure 4F,G) when neurite pruning was maximal (Figure 1C), but was re-established at 48 hr APF (Figure 4H,I) when neurite regrowth was occurring (Figure 1D) and maintained into the adult (Figure 4J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by t-GRASP data shown in Figure 4J,K.

claim: Control flies only expressing pre-t-GRASP in MDN did not have detectable t-GRASP signal at any timepoint.
source: Across each timepoint, control flies only expressing pre-t-GRASP in MDN did not have detectable t-GRASP signal (Figure 4F,H and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by control t-GRASP experiments shown in Figure 4F,H,J.

claim: MDN-Pair1 larval connectivity is established twice during development: initially established in the late embryo, and then re-established in the pupae.
source: Thus, MDN-Pair1 larval connectivity is established twice during development: initially established in the late embryo, and then re-established in the pupae.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the t-GRASP data and prior knowledge of embryonic development.

claim: A core interneuron circuit is preserved from larval stages into the adult.
source: Together with our earlier work (Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018), our results here show that a core interneuron circuit is preserved from larval stages into the adult.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in this manuscript and prior work.

claim: The preserved neuronal circuit contains MDN and its monosynaptically coupled Pair1 neuron, allowing the fly to switch between antagonistic behaviors: forward versus backward locomotion.
source: This neuronal circuit contains MDN and its monosynaptically coupled Pair1 neuron, allowing the fly to switch between antagonistic behaviors: forward versus backward locomotion.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in this manuscript.

claim: The larval circuit contains the MDN partners Pair1, ThDN, and A18b, and the Pair1 partner A27h.
source: The larval circuit contains the MDN partners Pair1, ThDN, and A18b, and the Pair1 partner A27h (Figure 5; Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: It is unlikely that MDN and A18b are synaptic partners during adulthood because MDN axons do not extend to the abdominal ganglion.
source: Although two independent A18b Gal4 lines have extensive off-target expression, permanently labeling the Gal4 expression during larval stages consistently labels an adult neuron in the abdominal ganglion (data not shown); since MDN axons do not extend to the abdominal ganglion, it is unlikely that MDN and A18b are synaptic partners during adulthood.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial separation of MDN axons and A18b location.

claim: The A27h interneuron undergoes apoptosis during pupal stages.
source: Additionally, the A27h interneuron, which regulates forward crawling in the larvae, undergoes apoptosis during pupal stages (data not shown) and thus cannot regulate forward walking in the adult.
evidence: This claim is based on unpublished observations by the authors.

claim: A27h cannot regulate forward walking in the adult because it undergoes apoptosis during pupal stages.
source: Additionally, the A27h interneuron, which regulates forward crawling in the larvae, undergoes apoptosis during pupal stages (data not shown) and thus cannot regulate forward walking in the adult.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that A27h undergoes apoptosis.

claim: The A27h neurons are located in the abdominal segments, which do not have a role in adult walking.
source: This is not surprising as the A27h neurons are located in the abdominal segments, which do not have a role in adult walking.
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge of Drosophila locomotion.

claim: Recent work mapping the adult MDN circuit has identified over 30 VNC neurons downstream of MDN, including the LBL40 and LUL130 neurons required for hindleg backward stepping.
source: Recent work mapping the adult MDN circuit has identified over 30 VNC neurons downstream of MDN, including the LBL40 and LUL130 neurons required for hindleg backward stepping (Figure 5; Feng et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent published work.

claim: Recent work has identified adult neurons important for forward walking.
source: Recent work has also identified adult neurons important for forward walking (Bidaye et al., 2020), but their relationship to adult MDN is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent published work.

claim: The relationship of adult forward walking neurons to adult MDN is unknown.
source: Recent work has also identified adult neurons important for forward walking (Bidaye et al., 2020), but their relationship to adult MDN is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Initiation of forward walking requires the forelegs, innervated by motor neurons in the prothoracic segment.
source: Elegant recent work has shown that initiation of forward walking requires the forelegs, innervated by motor neurons in the prothoracic segment, whereas initiation of backward walking requires the hindlegs, innervated by motor neuron in the metathoracic segment (Feng et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent published work.

claim: Initiation of backward walking requires the hindlegs, innervated by motor neurons in the metathoracic segment.
source: Elegant recent work has shown that initiation of forward walking requires the forelegs, innervated by motor neurons in the prothoracic segment, whereas initiation of backward walking requires the hindlegs, innervated by motor neuron in the metathoracic segment (Feng et al., 2020).
